prompt: Why does turning on `pg_stat_statements` need a restart of the server?
hint: Which setting names it?

choices.text: It is loaded at start-up, through `shared_preload_libraries`
choices.why: Right: it hooks into the code that runs every query, and a library preloaded at start-up is only read then.

choices.text: CREATE EXTENSION only works on a server that has just started
choices.why: CREATE EXTENSION works at any time; it is the library that needs the start-up.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM rewrites postgresql.conf and the restart re-reads it
choices.why: ALTER SYSTEM writes postgresql.auto.conf, and most settings it writes need only a reload.

choices.text: The statistics from before the restart would otherwise be mixed in with the new ones
choices.why: There are no statistics before it is loaded; the restart is about loading the code.

prompt: A screen runs `SELECT … WHERE customer_id = 17`, then `= 90210`, then `= 5`. How many rows does `pg_stat_statements` hold for them?
hint: Constants are taken out before the statements are compared.

choices.text: Three, one per value
choices.why: That would make the tally useless for an application that sends a million values.

choices.text: One, with three calls
choices.why: Right: all three are `WHERE customer_id = $1`, one queryid.

choices.text: None until the statement has run a hundred times
choices.why: A statement is counted from its first run.

choices.text: Two: one for small values and one for large ones
choices.why: The extension does not group by value at all; it removes the values.

prompt: `\timing` said a query took 1.3 ms and `mean_exec_time` says 0.9 ms for the same statement. What explains the difference?
hint: Who measures each number, and from where?

choices.text: One of the two is wrong and the server should be restarted
choices.why: Both are right; they measure different stretches of time.

choices.text: The tally rounds its numbers down
choices.why: It keeps full precision, as the expanded row in the lesson shows.

choices.text: The server's figure leaves out the trip across the connection
choices.why: Right: psql measures from sending to receiving; the server only its own execution.

choices.text: `\timing` includes the time spent planning other people's queries
choices.why: Other sessions' work is not in anybody's timing of this query.

prompt: To make the next numbers count from zero, call `pg_stat_statements____()`.
hint: The function the first fix calls before building the index.

prompt: Match each column of `pg_stat_statements` to what it says.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: how many times the statement ran
the sum of every run, in milliseconds
pages asked of the operating system
how spread out the runs were

right_distractors: the moment the statement last ran

prompt: In `pgbench -f customer-orders.sql@50 -f order-page.sql@25 …`, what does `@50` mean?
hint: Out of every hundred transactions.

choices.text: Fifty clients run that script
choices.why: The number of clients is `-c`; the weight is about the mix.

choices.text: Its weight: half of all transactions
choices.why: Right: pgbench picks each transaction's script in proportion to the weights.

choices.text: Run it for fifty seconds
choices.why: Duration is `-T`, and applies to the whole run.

choices.text: Stop after fifty transactions of this script
choices.why: That would be `-t` for the whole run; weights do not stop anything.

prompt: Why does the workload include `place-order.sql`, which writes, when every question in this lesson is about reading?
hint: What would a read-only workload hide?

choices.text: pgbench refuses to run a workload with no writes in it
choices.why: It runs any script, read-only ones included.

choices.text: Because writes make the reads faster
choices.why: Writes compete with reads for the same server.

choices.text: So that the cost of locks and of maintaining indexes is part of the picture
choices.why: Right: an index that speeds a read is paid for on every write, and only a workload with writes shows it.

choices.text: To fill the tables before the reads start
choices.why: The tables were filled by market.sql; the writes run at the same time as the reads.

prompt: Your run reports 400 transactions a second where the lesson's reported 912, but the same three scripts are the slowest. What does that tell you?
hint: What the lesson says should match, and what should not.

choices.text: Your setup is broken and must be rebuilt
choices.why: A slower machine produces exactly this: different digits, same shape.

choices.text: The workload files were copied wrong
choices.why: A wrong file would change which scripts are slow, not just the rate.

choices.text: Nothing: same shape, different machine
choices.why: Right: rates depend on processors and disk; the ranking depends on the queries.

choices.text: pgbench needs `-j` raised to match the lesson
choices.why: Threads do not turn two processors into four.

prompt: Out of every hundred transactions in the workload, how many are a refresh of the operations screen?
hint: The weight after `pending-count.sql`.

prompt: Which question does sorting `pg_stat_statements` by `total_exec_time` answer?
hint: Total against mean.

choices.text: Which statement takes the most of the server's time
choices.why: Right: the total is what a statement takes away from everybody else.

choices.text: How long one user waits for the slowest screen of the application
choices.why: That is what the mean says, for one statement.

choices.text: Which statement failed most often
choices.why: The tally counts executions, not failures.

choices.text: Which statement returned the most rows to the application
choices.why: That is the `rows` column, a different question.

prompt: In the lesson's minute, the pending count averaged 221 ms and the tag search 30 ms, yet the tag search was first by total. Why?
hint: Multiply.

choices.text: The tag search ran about ten times more
choices.why: Right: 5497 runs against 540, and the total is calls times mean.

choices.text: The pending count's runs were cancelled before they finished
choices.why: No transaction failed in the run, and cancelled runs would not explain a ranking.

choices.text: The total counts planning time and the mean does not
choices.why: Both come from the same execution times.

choices.text: The tally overestimates queries on small tables
choices.why: It measures; it does not estimate.

prompt: A statement runs at 0.11 ms, 27489 times a minute, and another at 200 ms once an hour. You can make either one twice as fast. Which gives the server more time back in a day?
hint: Work out each one's total for a day.

choices.text: The 200 ms one: a fix to a slow query is always worth more
choices.why: Halving it saves 100 ms an hour, 2.4 seconds a day.

choices.text: Neither: both are too small to matter
choices.why: One of them is over an hour of server time a day.

choices.text: The 0.11 ms one, by a wide margin
choices.why: Right: 27489 × 1440 × 0.055 ms is over half an hour a day; the other saves seconds.

choices.text: They are about equal
choices.why: One is minutes, the other seconds.

prompt: The seller dashboard's row shows 2164 calls and a mean of 35.49 ms. To the nearest second, how much server time did it take in that minute?
hint: calls × mean.

prompt: The seller dashboard's fastest run took 12 ms and its slowest 116 ms, with a standard deviation of 14.8 around a mean of 35.5. What is the most likely reason?
hint: The statement is the same; what changes between runs?

choices.text: The disk was failing during the slow runs
choices.why: Only 1181 pages came from outside memory; the disk barely took part.

choices.text: Its cost depends on which seller was asked about
choices.why: Right: a seller with more December orders makes more rows to read and sum.

choices.text: pgbench measured it wrongly
choices.why: These numbers come from the server, not from pgbench.

choices.text: The planner chose a different index on each run, at random
choices.why: The planner is deterministic for the same statistics; nothing is drawn at random.

prompt: Why does the lesson reset the tally before building the index and running the workload again?
hint: A tally always has a start.

choices.text: Building an index is refused while the tally holds rows
choices.why: The two are unrelated; CREATE INDEX does not look at the tally.

choices.text: So the after numbers count only the minute after the fix
choices.why: Right: otherwise the after would be averaged with the before.

choices.text: To free memory for the new index
choices.why: The tally's memory is fixed and tiny next to an index.

choices.text: Because pg_stat_statements forgets everything after 5000 calls of one statement
choices.why: 5000 is the number of distinct statements, not of calls.

prompt: After the seller index, the dashboard's share of the server fell from 21% to 7%, but the workload's overall rate only went from 912 to 972 transactions a second. Why so little?
hint: How often does the dashboard run?

choices.text: The index was not used
choices.why: The dashboard's mean fell from 35 to 11 ms, which only the index explains.

choices.text: pgbench is limited to a thousand transactions a second
choices.why: There is no such limit; the rate depends on the work.

choices.text: Writing the index slowed every other query by the same amount
choices.why: Only writes maintain an index, and they are a tenth of the workload.

choices.text: It is four transactions in a hundred, and two other heavy statements still dominate
choices.why: Right: a large gain on a small part of the mix is a small gain on the whole.

prompt: Put the lesson's first fix in the order it was done.
hint: Measure, change one thing, measure the same way.
items: Run the workload and sort the tally by total
Pick the statement a known structure fixes
Run the same workload for the same minute and compare
trap: Resetting after building would put the build itself in the before; changing before measuring leaves nothing to compare against.

prompt: When does the lesson tell you to run `~/reset-market.sh`?
hint: The workload wrote orders.

choices.text: Before every query
choices.why: It drops and copies 1.3 GB; it is for getting back to known rows, not for every query.

choices.text: When your numbers drift from the transcripts, or a lesson says so
choices.why: Right: it puts market back as lesson 3 starts.

choices.text: Only after the server crashes
choices.why: A crash does not change the rows; the workload does.

choices.text: Once, at the end of the course
choices.why: Lessons that change the rows ask for it as they go.

prompt: Which question can the log answer and `pg_stat_statements` cannot?
hint: One keeps the values.

choices.text: Which statement costs the server the most over a day
choices.why: That is arithmetic over all runs, the tally's job.

choices.text: How many times a statement ran in the last minute
choices.why: `calls` answers that directly.

choices.text: For which seller one slow run of the dashboard was
choices.why: Right: the log writes the statement with its real values, `seller_id = 21`.

choices.text: The average time of the tag search
choices.why: `mean_exec_time` is exactly that.

prompt: Why is `log_min_duration_statement = 0` left on only for a short window?
hint: What does each line cost?

choices.text: It needs a full restart of the server to be switched off again
choices.why: It changes with a reload, as the lesson did.

choices.text: It logs everything, which costs a write per statement
choices.why: Right: a thousand statements a second is a thousand writes a second to a file on the same disk.

choices.text: Zero disables the log entirely
choices.why: Zero logs everything; -1 is what disables it.

choices.text: The log forgets entries older than a minute, so a long window shows nothing
choices.why: The log is a file; it keeps what is written until it is rotated.

prompt: Which of these can `pg_stat_statements` NOT tell you? Choose all that apply.
hint: Five blind spots.

choices.text: How long the application waited for a free connection
choices.why: Right: that wait is in front of the server, outside execution.

choices.text: Whether a page it read from the operating system came from the disk
choices.why: Right: `shared_blks_read` cannot tell the OS cache from the disk.

choices.text: Which customer a slow run was for
choices.why: Right: the values are taken out.

choices.text: How many times a statement ran
choices.why: That is `calls`.

choices.text: The slowest run of a statement
choices.why: That is `max_exec_time`.

prompt: An application builds its SQL by pasting values into strings. In `pg_stat_statements_info`, `dealloc` climbs every hour. What is happening to the tally?
hint: What happens when the table of distinct statements is full?

choices.text: Nothing to worry about: dealloc counts statements that were planned twice
choices.why: It counts evictions of entries from a full table.

choices.text: It is churning, and rare expensive statements are the ones being evicted
choices.why: Right: least-used entries go first, and a rare expensive query is least used.

choices.text: The server is running out of memory and will stop
choices.why: The table has a fixed size; evicting is how it stays that size.

choices.text: pgbench is running in the background and filling the table with entries
choices.why: pgbench has nothing to do with eviction.

prompt: A page of the shop takes three seconds, and the tally shows nothing above 2 ms on average, with one statement called 120 times per page view. Which suspect from lesson 1 and which fix?
hint: A cheap statement called many times.

choices.text: The query: the page should ask once for what it now asks 120 times
choices.why: Right: the N+1 shape is a design problem; no index removes 120 round trips.

choices.text: The schema: an index on the statement's column
choices.why: At under 2 ms a call the statement already finds its rows fast.

choices.text: The machine: more processors for the database server
choices.why: The server is idle most of those three seconds, waiting for the next of 120 requests.

choices.text: None, because the tally shows nothing slow
choices.why: Read calls as well as time: 120 a page is the finding.
